Every cell asserts the same both-sided budget the current rows assert; today's rows only ever use `records: []`, which is the one shape the pre-check gets right.

summary: `disconnect()` landing inside an in-flight `connect()` is silently discarded: `connect()` finishes by assigning `this.nc`, resetting `this.stopped = false` and bumping the epoch, so the plugin ends the sequence fully live with `stopped === false`. `connect()`'s own guard names exactly this hazard ("would strand the previous connection, whose unbounded reconnect loop keeps its socket alive"), and `maxReconnectAttempts: -1` means the stranded socket never gives up.
failure: const p = new NatsPlugin(); const c = p.connect({servers:'127.0.0.1:14222'}); await p.disconnect(); await c; -> internal `nc` is present and `nc.isClosed() === false`, `stopped === false`. The caller that already awaited `disconnect()` holds an object it believes is torn down; a caller that then drops the reference leaks an open socket with an unbounded reconnect loop.
remediation: Capture the epoch at `connect()` entry and, if it changed while the connect was in flight, close the new connection and leave `nc`/`stopped` as teardown left them (or reject the connect) rather than publishing live handles.
testUpgrade: Add a lifecycle table sweeping `disconnect()` across every await point of `connect()` (before `connect`, between `connect` and `jetstreamManager`, after), each asserting the same invariant: once `disconnect()` resolves, `nc` is closed or absent and `stopped` is true. The same table shape should cover `connect()` racing `subscribe()`/`fetchRecent()`, so the class — teardown interleaved with setup — is guarded rather than this one offset.

summary: `wireTopic` case-folds and length-checks a topic but does not strip edge whitespace. Zulip's send endpoint declares `topic` as `OptionalTopic = Annotated[str|None, StringConstraints(strip_whitespace=True)]` (zerver/lib/typed_endpoint.py:109-113), so it silently rewrites the subject, while every read/register narrow matches with `Q(subject__iexact=topic_name)` (zerver/lib/topic.py:409) and does NOT strip. A topic with a leading/trailing space (or U+00A0/U+2003/U+3000 — Python `str.strip()` removes all of them) is therefore WRITE-ONLY, and the `claimedWireTopics` collision guard — which exists precisely to stop two Parley topics sharing one Zulip history — keys on the un-stripped name and never fires.
failure: `post(asTopic('ctx-handoff-abc '), h, 'the hand-off')` resolves with a durable id (1). `fetchRecent({topic: 'ctx-handoff-abc '})` returns `{messages: [], nextCursor: '0'}` forever and `subscribe('ctx-handoff-abc ', …)` delivers nothing — reproduced in the worktree after teaching the fake the documented strip. Separately, `post('ctx-handoff-abc ')` and `post('ctx-handoff-abc')` both succeed and the second topic's `fetchRecent` returns BOTH messages: two distinct Parley topics silently merged into one history with no collision error. The fake models `truncateTopic` but not the strip, and `SERVER_CONSTRAINTS` does not list it, so no existing test can see either half.
remediation: Normalize the topic in `wireTopic` exactly as the server does and take the same arm the plugin already takes for over-long topics and rewritten bodies: compute `topic.trim().toLowerCase()`, and if it differs from `topic.toLowerCase()`, throw naming what the server would store (or, if silent normalization is preferred, claim and narrow on the STRIPPED name so post/read/register agree and the collision registry keys on the wire truth). Also reject a name that strips to empty. Add `stripsTopicEdges: true` to the fake's `SERVER_CONSTRAINTS` and implement it in `truncateTopic`, so the existing "every modelled server constraint is claimed by a write row" assertion forces the guard.

summary: The push loop is bound to `this.generation` so it cannot be resurrected by the next `connect()`. summary: `reconnect()`'s exponential backoff applies only to dial FAILURES. A Socket Mode edge that accepts, greets, and then closes (a flapping proxy, a load-balancer drain, an app_token at its ~10-connection quota being reaped) makes every dial SUCCEED, so `backoffMs` never advances and `ensureSocket()` returns immediately — the loop redials `apps.connections.open` at the round-trip rate of the edge.
failure: Probe: `startSlack()`, `subscribe(topic)`, then `setInterval(() => fake.dropSockets(), 50)` for 4 s with no blocked fetch at all -> 79 `apps.connections.open` calls in 4 s (~20/s). `apps.connections.open` is Slack Tier 1 (~1 request/minute); the plugin's own JSDoc at src/index.ts:653 and :692 calls it "Slack's tightest-limit endpoint". Real Slack answers 429 and, under sustained abuse, rate-limit-disables the app. `dialCooldownUntil` cannot help: `ensureSocket()`'s success arm resets it to 0 (src/index.ts:674).

Equivalently, gate every `openSocket()` on `dialCooldownUntil` (not just the poll path) and set that cooldown on socket LOSS as well as on dial failure.

Each row runs a fixed wall-clock window and asserts `fake.hits('apps.connections.open') <= ceil(window / DIAL_BACKOFF_MS) + 2`. `connection-lifecycle.test.ts`'s OUTAGES table is too narrow to have caught this: every one of its rows makes the dial or the handshake FAIL, which is the one path that already has a cooldown.

summary: `blockForMessage`'s ladder bounds the TIMEOUT exit of each rung but not the WAKE exit. `drainWaiters()` (src/index.ts:815, fired on every established-socket close) resolves the rung waiter immediately, and the loop head re-queries `conversations.history` at once with no floor. summary: The degradation table's request ceiling `rungStarts(DEGRADED_BLOCK_MS).length + 2` is a magic slack over a real clock, asserted inside a suite that runs files in parallel. summary: `nextSeq` is reconstructed ONLY from the record lines that survive a load, while the `#epoch` identity survives independently. Any partial loss of records (crash-torn tail, a garbled line the loader drops, a stale/rolled-back copy) lowers the high-water below cursors already handed out, and the store then re-mints those exact sequences under the SAME identity. Neither guard in `requireOwnCursor` fires: the epoch matches, and once new traffic pushes the high-water back past the held cursor the `ahead of every message this store has observed` check stops firing too. The result is the permanently short page that cursor-lifecycle.test.ts's own header calls the one unacceptable answer, and no Bot API call can ever hand those messages back.
failure: Reproduced end-to-end through the plugin. Post a,b,c,d to topic -1009800904; the agent holds d's cursor <epoch>.4. Disconnect; drop the last record line from the store file (keeping every '#' bookkeeping line, i.e. same identity). Restart, post 'e' then 'f' (stamped seq 4 and 5 - seq 4 is REUSED). fetchRecent({topic, since:'<epoch>.4', limit:100}) returns ['f'] with nextCursor <epoch>.5. Message 'e' is silently and permanently unreachable - no throw, no diagnostic. Same class at store level: append 5 records, hand out <epoch>.5, truncate the file mid-last-line, reopen, append -> the new record is again <epoch>.5.

The store must never re-issue a sequence it has already stamped under an identity it keeps.

summary: ObservedStore's class doc declares ONE bridge process per store file as structurally unsupported, but nothing enforces it: no advisory lock, no pidfile, no O_EXCL claim, no error. Worse, defaultStorePath() is a single fixed absolute path that does not depend on the bot token or bot id - so the README's own recommended multi-session deployment (provision one bot per session) puts N processes on ONE store file under default config. Two stores then load the same #epoch and the same nextSeq, mint colliding cursors for different messages, and either one's compaction (a rename over the path) discards the history the other wrote.
failure: Reproduced. (a) new ObservedStore(path,2) twice on one path, one append each: both return seq 1 under the same identity, so two different messages carry the identical cursor fa26afc5cdede0d1.1. (b) new ObservedStore(path,1) twice; B appends B1..B4, then A appends A1..A4 (A compacts and renames its view over the path). Re-reading the file shows only #epoch, #evicted and A's record - B1..B4 are gone from disk permanently, and the Bot API has no history endpoint to backfill them. No error and no stderr line on either side.
remediation: Claim the store file exclusively at construction - an flock/O_EXCL lock sibling (<store_path>.lock carrying the pid) released on close(), with a stale-lock check - and fail connect naming the path and the holding pid rather than corrupting silently. Independently make defaultStorePath() per-bot (e.g. .../telegram/<getMe id>/observed.jsonl, or a hash of the token) so two legitimately provisioned bots on one host never collide by default, and say so in the README's Multiple concurrent sessions section.

summary: post resolves the topic to a canonical chat id via chatIdFor -> canonicalChatId (normalised through BigInt), but then ingests, wakes waiters, fans out to subscribers and checks its own durability guard under String(sent.chat.id) taken from the sendMessage RESPONSE. The two normalisations differ, so whenever they disagree the record lands in a chat bucket the topic never queries - and store.has(sentId), the guard whose whole purpose is to stop post resolving with a backendMsgId no fetchRecent will ever return, passes vacuously because it uses the same wrong key. canonicalChatId's JSDoc claims BigInt is there so a chat id past Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is not rounded on the way through; the inbound/echo half rounds it, defeating that claim. requireMessage also deliberately accepts a STRING chat.id, which ingest then uses unnormalised.
failure: Reproduced against the in-process fake. topic = '9007199254740993' (2^53+1). subscribe(topic, ...) then post(topic, SENDER, 'hello') RESOLVES with '9007199254740992:1' - an id whose chat half is not even the topic's chat id. fetchRecent({topic, limit:100}) returns {messages: [], nextCursor: '<epoch>.0'} and the live subscriber receives nothing. The topic is a permanent black hole while every seam call reports success. Same shape for a chat.id echoed as a non-canonical string ('-0012345') and for a supergroup migration whose response names a different chat.
remediation: Index, wake and fan out under the chat id the TOPIC resolved to rather than the response's echo - or, if the echo must win, run it through the same canonicalChatId normalisation and reject the post loudly when the normalised response id differs from the resolved chat id (naming both), so a redirected chat is a visible failure instead of a silent black hole. Apply the same normalisation to String(message.chat.id) on the getUpdates path.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a chat-id-key-agreement case over the spellings an upstream can put on chat.id - number in range, number past MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, numeric string, '-00123' string, a different chat id than the one addressed - x each ingest path {sendMessage response, getUpdates update} x each observer {fetchRecent on the addressed topic, a live subscriber on it}. Invariant: either the message is reachable through the topic that addressed it, or the seam call rejects naming both ids. This needs the fake widened to echo chat.id verbatim in each spelling; today enqueue/buildChat always stamp a rounded JS number, which is why the whole class is unreachable from the suite.

summary: openRig() hands back a restart() that connects an additional plugin (new poll loop, new store fd) but its close() disconnects only the ORIGINAL plugin. startRig()'s same-named restart() is correct - it goes through connectTo, which registers teardown - so two rigs in one file give the same method opposite lifetime contracts. The only current consumer (conformance.test.ts) never calls openRig().restart(), so the leak is latent: the first test that does gets a stray getUpdates loop and an unclosed store descriptor outliving the case, which on this package surfaces as someone else's poll-count or fd assertion going red.
failure: const rig = await openRig(); const p2 = await rig.restart(); await rig.close(); leaves p2 connected - its poll loop keeps calling the (now closed) fake and openFdsFor(rig.storePath) stays non-zero. The identical sequence through startRig tears both plugins down.
remediation: Have openRig track every plugin it connects and disconnect them all in close(), newest-first - the same LIFO contract startRig inherits from the module-level cleanups array - or drop restart from openRig entirely, since its one consumer does not use it.
testUpgrade: Add a rig self-test parameterized over both rigs that asserts the teardown CONTRACT rather than plugin behaviour: for each of {startRig, openRig}, connect, call restart() twice, run teardown, then assert openFdsFor(storePath) === 0 and that the fake's getUpdates call count is frozen over a following 500ms window. docs.test.ts already lints rig duplication out; this pins that the two rigs also agree on lifetime.

summary: A credential carried in a query value that contains an unencoded `+` survives redaction, because `URLSearchParams` decodes `+` to a space and none of the three spellings `spellings()` generates reproduce the raw form.
failure: fetchWithRetry('https://h.example/v1/x?access_token=AAAAbbbb+CCCCdddd+EEEE', {}, {label:'L', isStopped:()=>false}) against a 404 whose body echoes the value alone -> thrown message is `L → 404: no route for AAAAbbbb+CCCCdddd+EEEE`. credentialParts() sees the decoded value 'AAAAbbbb CCCCdddd EEEE' and emits it, its %20 form, and itself — never the `+` form that is actually on the wire and in the body. Standard (non-url-safe) base64 API keys contain `+`, and the message becomes an MCP isError result, i.e. model context and operator logs.
remediation: Derive query-value spellings from the RAW query text as well as the decoded value: split `parsed.search.slice(1)` on '&'/'=' and feed each raw value through carriesSecret/spellings alongside searchParams.values(). Equivalently add `part.replaceAll(' ', '+')` to spellings(), but the raw-substring approach also covers `%2F`, `;` and any other normalization the URL parser applies.
testUpgrade: Generalize the SHAPED_LOCATIONS x SHAPES table so the echoed fragment is the RAW substring of `new URL(url).search`/`.pathname`, not the value the test wrote — that catches every spelling the parser normalizes, not just `+`. Widen ALPHABETS with a standard-base64 alphabet ('ABC…+/=') and a percent-bearing one; today's rows are all `+`-free (base64url, base62, hex, base32, alphabetic, dotted JWT), which is exactly why 60+ green cells miss this.

summary: The wall-clock `budget <= 0` exit inside the retry loop throws a plain `Error` with no `status` field, so `statusOf()` returns undefined for a rejection raised after a 429 was received — contradicting the README and the class error-envelope.test.ts says it guards.
failure: Reproduced: stub a permanent 429 with `Retry-After: 0.2` and call fetchWithRetry with deadlineMs=201 (and 202) — the loop passes the `elapsed + wait > deadlineMs` check, sleeps 200 ms, the sleep overshoots, and the next iteration takes `budget <= 0`. Result: message `L → deadline: exceeded 201ms before attempt 2`, `err.name === 'Error'`, `statusOf(err) === undefined`. A caller branching on 429 (bridge-telegram's fatal-status branch, any backoff ladder) silently stops firing, and the operator loses both the 429 and the 'Raise deadlineMs to wait it out' guidance. README lines 26-30 explicitly promise 'every rejection raised *after* a status arrived reports it … including `→ deadline:`'.
remediation: Carry the last received status through the loop and throw `new LabelledError(...)` (or an HttpStatusError for 429) from the `budget <= 0` branch, and word it as the rate-limit exhaustion it is when the previous attempt was a 429.
testUpgrade: Parameterize error-envelope.test.ts's 'a rejection after the status is known reports that status' table over the LOOP's own exits, not just the read-path ones: {attempt cap, stated wait past deadline, budget exhausted before the next attempt, disconnect mid-backoff, oversized body, mid-stream death} x {429, 404, 500}. Drive the budget-exhausted row deterministically with an injected `now` that advances by the real elapsed wait so the row does not depend on a ~1 ms timer-overshoot window.

summary: The only assertion proving a `supportsBlockingFetch: true` plugin actually blocks — `expect(Date.now() - idleStarted).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(150)` — has no BROKEN_VARIANTS control, so it can be deleted with the whole package, negative control included, staying green.
failure: Mutation run: replaced that line with `void idleStarted;` and ran `npx vitest run packages/conformance` — 412/412 tests passed (97 s, including the PARLEY_CONFORMANCE_BROKEN child run). Traced why: of the three native-blocking variants, 'returns at the budget instead of on the message' and 'parks from now instead of at the caller cursor' both fail earlier in arm (a); 'whose cursor moves on an empty timeout' really does block 300 ms and fails on the cursor instead. So a plugin declaring native blockMs support that returns instantly on an empty page is certified, and the ASSERTED_PROPERTIES registry — built for exactly this level — has no entry for it.
remediation: Add an ASSERTED_PROPERTIES entry (e.g. 'native-block-actually-waits') and a BROKEN_VARIANTS row declaring `supportsBlockingFetch: true` whose fetchRecent returns the inner page immediately even when `blockMs` is set and the page is empty, with `mustFail: 'blockMs is honoured natively or ignored promptly'`.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS mechanically rather than adding one variant: make the negative control require a variant per ASSERTED_PROPERTY *per capability arm* (it already does flag x arm x clause, but not property x arm), and derive ASSERTED_PROPERTIES membership for any assertion whose subject is elapsed TIME — i.e. add a suite-shape row asserting every `toBeGreaterThanOrEqual`/`toBeLessThan` over `Date.now() - <start>` in the suite names a property in ASSERTED_PROPERTIES, so the next timing clause cannot arrive uncontrolled.

summary: `cases()` keys on `/^ {4}it(?:\.each)?\(/gm`, so any case nested one level deeper (inside a `describe` within `runConformanceSuite`) is invisible to every meta-check in the package — skip detection, capability-guard assertions, deferred-promise handling, self-imposed budgets, the CLAUSES 1:1 count, README advertising, and the negative control's clause↔variant mapping.
failure: Mutation run: injected `describe('an ungraded clause', () => { it('grades nothing and no meta-check can see it', async () => { const t = ctx.freshTopic(); await ctx.plugin.post(t, SENDER, 'x'); }); });` inside runConformanceSuite before the 'topics are isolated' case. suite-shape.test.ts and readme.test.ts stayed green (120/120): `cases()` still returned 21, so `expect(cases()).toHaveLength(CLAUSES.length)` passed, the new case needed no CLAUSES row, no README bullet, and no BROKEN_VARIANTS control — while it runs against all eleven certified backends asserting nothing.
remediation: Parse cases by scanning for `it(`/`it.each(` at ANY indentation inside the `runConformanceSuite` body (or count the registrations at runtime via a vitest `describe` introspection / a stub of `it`), rather than by a fixed four-space prefix.

That is the same shape as the multi-line `it.each` row that was added after the last parser bug, so it durably ratchets the class rather than this instance.

summary: The README claims 'These live here so the backends that warn about the same thing share one classifier: a security predicate copied per backend is a predicate fixed in one place and left wrong in the others' — but bridge-discord ships its own `plaintextRemoteOrigin` with the opposite fail direction, because the shared one's `string | undefined` return cannot carry the 'use X instead' scheme Discord's warning needs.
failure: packages/bridge-discord/src/index.ts:1147 defines a local `plaintextRemoteOrigin(raw)` returning `{origin, secure}`, keyed on a PLAINTEXT_SCHEMES allowlist — so a scheme neither side knows classifies as SAFE there (undefined) while the shared one warns, and it prints `URL.origin`, which is the literal string 'null' for an unknown scheme (the exact hazard net-util's own comment at src/index.ts:636 says it avoids by building the origin by hand). bridge-discord imports `isLoopbackHost` from this package, so half the predicate is shared and half is forked.
remediation: Widen the shared classifier so the fork is unnecessary — e.g. return `{ origin, secure } | undefined` with a `SECURE_FOR` map (`http:`->`https:`, `ws:`->`wss:`, unknown -> a generic 'use a TLS scheme' hint) while keeping the fail-safe direction — then delete the Discord copy. Until that lands, drop or qualify the README sentence: it is a public npm claim that is currently false.
testUpgrade: Add a repo-wide row to this package's README/consumer tests: for every package that imports anything from `@sharptrick/parley-net-util`, assert its `src/**` declares no local function whose name collides with an export of this module. That guards the CLASS (a shared predicate silently re-implemented per backend) rather than the Discord instance, and it fails the day the next fork appears.

summary: README: 'Userinfo takes neither exemption: it is credential-by-construction, so a short password is redacted too.' The code applies a `part.length > 1` filter to every credential part including userinfo, so a one-character password is not redacted.
failure: Reproduced: fetchWithRetry('https://user:q@h.example/v1/x', …) against a 401 whose body is 'bad creds q for user' yields `L → 401: bad creds q for <redacted>` — the username 'user' is struck, the password 'q' survives verbatim.
remediation: Either exempt `username`/`password` from the `length > 1` filter (they are credential-by-construction, which is what the doc asserts), or soften the README sentence to state the actual bound. The former matches the stated intent; note that a 1-char redaction target would strike single letters out of the body, which is presumably why the filter exists — so say so.

The same axis applied to the path/query rows would pin where the documented exemptions actually start, so a bound moving in code fails the row rather than the prose.

summary: The CLAUSES↔README ratchet only runs one way: every entry in CLAUSES must appear in the README, but nothing asserts that every clause-shaped bullet in the README is still in CLAUSES. A clause can be retired (case + CLAUSES row + its BROKEN_VARIANTS entry removed consistently) with the README still advertising it.
failure: Delete the 'post accepts inReplyTo' case, its CLAUSES entry and its 'a post that rejects a threaded reply' variant: the orphan-variant check passes (no orphan), the 1:1 count check passes (both sides shrank), and readme.test.ts's `it.each(CLAUSES)('advertises the clause %s')` never looks at the leftover README bullet. The README then documents to npm consumers a guarantee eleven certified backends are no longer graded on — the precise failure mode the CLAUSES table was introduced to prevent.
remediation: Add the reverse assertion: extract the clause bullet list from the README (the block under 'checks the clauses below') and require every bullet to be matched by a CLAUSES entry, so a retired clause forces a README edit in the same change.

The regression only surfaced downstream — 262 failures across 26 other backend test files (535 s) — i.e. every consumer's ordinary catch-up page (Matrix /sync, Slack conversations.history, Zulip /messages) would start failing with `→ body: response body exceeded 1024 bytes`, and the owning package's 509-case suite would not name it.

summary: `MIN_HASH_LEN = 10` is both the floor and the DEFAULT suffix width, so every shipped backend's topic→channel mapping rests on 40 bits of truncated SHA-1. The JSDoc states the cost honestly (2^(4 x hashLen)) but treats it as sufficient; 2^40 SHA-1 evaluations is roughly two minutes on one commodity GPU, and a hit routes one topic's traffic into another topic's backend channel.
failure: Take a victim topic whose fold is lossy — e.g. `team.frontend` on the NATS stream fold, minting `team_frontend-08edf065f7`. An attacker who can post to arbitrary topics (any deployment with a broad `post_topics` pattern, which allowlist.test.ts treats as legitimate config) searches raw topics `t` with `sanitize(t) === 'team_frontend'` — trivially many, since every character in the illegal set folds to `_` — until `sha1(t)[0..10] === '08edf065f7'`. At ~10^10 SHA-1/s that is ~110 seconds of GPU time. `safeName` then returns the victim's exact backend name for the attacker's topic, and posts/fetches on the attacker's topic land in the victim's Matrix room / NATS stream / XMPP MUC. Note the attack only reaches topics whose fold is lossy: a naturally-safe topic passes through bare and no branch-B output can equal it, which limits but does not remove the exposure. I have not built the GPU search, hence PLAUSIBLE.
remediation: Raise the DEFAULT to 16 hex (64 bits) while leaving `MIN_HASH_LEN` where it is for backward compatibility of existing channel names, and say in the doc that 10 is a legacy floor rather than a recommendation — or make the digest unguessable by keying it (HMAC over a per-deployment secret from `backend_config`), which removes the offline search entirely. Either way, restate the margin in bits and against GPU rates rather than as an abstract exponent.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "a truncated-digest width is a security parameter, not a formatting choice" in stated-bounds.test.ts: add a row that asserts the DEFAULT width (not just the floor) in bits, `4 * defaultHashLen >= 64`, alongside the existing MIN/MAX bound rows, and a golden-vector row per fold pinning names minted at the default so a width change is visibly a rename of every existing channel. Add a birthday-collision smoke case that mints names for N generated topics sharing one sanitized form and asserts distinctness, parameterized over hashLen so lowering it reddens with a concrete collision rather than only failing a literal.

summary: `this.pending` is the one store the eviction comment (lines 182-189) explicitly names as "state any anonymous caller can create by calling /authorize", yet it is the only anonymous-writable store with no cap. `clients` gets MAX_CLIENTS plus a two-tier eviction policy; `pending` grows one entry per unauthenticated /authorize and is reclaimed only by the 60s sweeper or a 5-minute TTL.
failure: An anonymous caller registers one client, then issues /authorize requests up to the SDK limiter's default 100-per-15-min per address. Each adds a `PendingConsent` (holding the full `OAuthClientInformationFull` and `AuthorizationParams`) that lives 5 minutes. Distributed across source addresses this is unbounded heap growth on a single-process, unpersisted server whose README (examples/self-host-remote/README.md:79) tells the operator to "give the one process more room rather than adding replicas" — with no cap, more room is not a bound.
remediation: Cap `pending` the way `clients` is capped, and shed by the same honest ordering already implemented: refuse or evict the oldest unapproved consent when the map is full. The existing `clientStates()`/`evictionCandidate()` machinery already classifies pending state as `ownerApproved: false`, so the policy is a small extension rather than a new concept.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS "an anonymous caller can grow an unbounded provider store". Add a table over every Map on ParleyOAuthProvider, classified by who can write to it (anonymous vs owner-approved — the same classification `CLIENT_STATES` in oauth-provider.test.ts already builds, and which already asserts every store is covered). For each anonymous-writable store, drive N+1 creations through its public entry point and assert the store size stays bounded. Driving it off the declared store list means a new store added later is covered the day it lands; today only `clients` has a cap test (oauth-provider.test.ts:304).

summary: reconnectListener re-LISTENs every channel on the new client BEFORE adoptListener publishes it, while releaseListen still routes its UNLISTEN to `this.listener` — the dead client for the whole of that window. A release landing inside the window deletes the `listens` entry and sends the UNLISTEN to a socket that is already gone, leaving the replacement connection permanently registered for a channel nothing needs.
failure: Two blocking fetchRecent waits parked on channels C1 and C2, no subscription. The listener drops; the reconnect loop LISTENs C1, then awaits LISTEN C2. During that await C1's blockMs timer fires: releaseListen drops refs to 0, deletes C1 from this.listens, and issues UNLISTEN "C1" on the dead old client (rejected, swallowed). The new connection keeps C1 LISTENed forever with no entry anywhere to undo it, so every future post to that topic wakes the process into a handler that finds neither a subscription nor a waiter. No message is lost, but the wakeups are permanent unless C1 is re-acquired. waiters.test.ts asserts exactly this property ('channel left LISTENed on the connection') but only on the non-reconnect paths.
remediation: Adopt the replacement client before re-issuing the LISTENs (or route releaseListen through the pending replacement rather than this.listener), and clear `this.listener` in the 'end' handler so a release during a blackout has no dead client to talk to. Simplest correct shape: re-LISTEN from this.listens after adoptListener, re-checking membership per channel so one released in between is skipped.
testUpgrade: Guard the CLASS `the connection's observed LISTEN-minus-UNLISTEN set is empty whenever no participant needs a channel — including across a reconnect`. Extend the existing observedChannels() invariant into a table parameterized over {1,2,3} channels × {waiter-only, waiter+subscription} × {release before the re-LISTEN loop, during it, after adoption}, driving the drop with the mocked client's 'end' event and a LISTEN delay wide enough to sit inside the loop, and asserting observedChannels() on the REPLACEMENT client so a leak only the new socket carries is visible.
